records.sourceFile: The Prevalence of High School Multi Sport Participation in Elite National Football League Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Steinl GK, Padaki AS, Irvine JN, et al. The prevalence of high school multi-sport participation in elite National Football League athletes. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2021;49(4):476-479.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort study described high-school sport participation among 318 NFL first-round draft selections from 2008 through 2017 and compared subsequent availability and career outcomes between multi-sport and football-only athletes.
paper.tldr: Most NFL first-round picks in this cohort played multiple high-school sports, but multi-sport and football-only groups did not differ significantly in games missed because of injury, games played, career length, or Pro Bowl selection. This is descriptive association evidence, not proof that specialization or diversification causes an NFL outcome.
paper.methods: Publicly available high-school participation histories and NFL career data were assembled for 318 first-round picks. Athletes were classified as multi-sport or football-only, then compared on injury-related games missed, total games, career longevity, and Pro Bowl selection.
paper.findings: Two hundred eighty athletes (88%) were classified as multi-sport and 38 (12%) as football-only. The authors found no statistically significant between-group differences in the measured NFL injury, availability, longevity, or achievement outcomes.
paper.limitations: Only 38 athletes were football-only, participation histories could be misclassified from public sources, injury reports lacked clinical detail, off-season injuries were not captured, and first-round picks are a highly selected population. Causality cannot be inferred.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use early sport specialization as a prerequisite for identifying football talent. Support broad youth sport participation when it fits the athlete, while recognizing that this study did not establish an injury-prevention or career-performance advantage.
paper.athleteDev: Multi-sport backgrounds were common among elite draft selections and can coexist with high football attainment. Preserve opportunities to develop varied movement, competition, and learning experiences without promising that participation pattern alone improves professional outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study does not test rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions. Do not use prior multi-sport status to estimate recovery time, reinjury risk, or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Performance enhancing drugs in healthy athletes - An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.pdf

paper.citation: Warrier AA, Azua EN, Kasson LB, et al. Performance-enhancing drugs in healthy athletes: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Sports Health. 2024;16(5):695-705.
paper.abstract: This umbrella review synthesized 27 systematic reviews and meta-analyses on creatine, anabolic-androgenic steroids, growth hormone, recombinant human erythropoietin, and cannabis in healthy athletes, considering both performance effects and adverse outcomes.
paper.tldr: Effects and harms differed sharply by agent. Creatine had the clearest support for strength and repeated high-intensity performance; anabolic steroids could increase strength and lean mass but carried health harms; growth hormone and cannabis lacked clear performance benefit; and erythropoietin evidence was limited alongside serious cardiovascular risk.
paper.methods: The authors searched PubMed and Scopus for systematic reviews and meta-analyses involving healthy athletes and five performance-related agents. Twenty-seven reviews were included, with findings summarized by agent and graded as level-4 evidence.
paper.findings: Creatine supported strength and repeated high-intensity performance. Anabolic-steroid reviews reported strength gains ranging from 5% to 52% and a lean-mass standardized mean difference of 0.62, alongside adverse lipid effects. Growth hormone improved body composition without clear performance benefit; recombinant erythropoietin evidence was sparse with serious cardiovascular risk; cannabis did not improve performance and could impair it.
paper.limitations: Only two databases were searched; included reviews were heterogeneous and often based on limited primary evidence. The umbrella review found no eligible review evidence for selective androgen receptor modulators or angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, and its broad agent-level summaries cannot define individual risk.
paper.practicalImplications: Separate permitted, evidence-supported supplementation from prohibited or high-risk drug use. Direct medication, supplement, and anti-doping questions to qualified medical and nutrition staff; never treat a performance effect as evidence of safety or eligibility.
paper.athleteDev: Build performance through training, recovery, nutrition, and transparent supplement governance. Creatine may be considered within individualized, independently tested protocols, while illicit or medically inappropriate agents require clear education on health, eligibility, and ethical consequences.
paper.rtp: This review does not establish return-to-sport protocols. Drug exposure, adverse effects, or suspected misuse requires medical assessment, and clearance should address organ-system risk and anti-doping status rather than perceived performance benefit.

records.sourceFile: The use of biologics in NFL athletes - An expert consensus of NFL team physicians.pdf

paper.citation: Murray IR, McAdams TR, Hammond KE, et al. The use of biologics in NFL athletes: An expert consensus of NFL team physicians. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(2):23259671221143778.
paper.abstract: This expert-consensus project used a three-round Delphi process to develop 47 statements about biologic treatments in NFL athletes, including platelet-rich plasma, bone-marrow-derived products, and other cell-based interventions.
paper.tldr: NFL team physicians reached consensus supporting selected platelet-rich-plasma uses, including patellar tendinopathy and symptom management in early osteoarthritis, while emphasizing that many cell products are marketed beyond the evidence. Consensus describes expert practice and judgment; it does not prove comparative efficacy.
paper.methods: A six-member working group developed statements that were rated through three Delphi rounds by physicians representing 26 NFL teams plus NFL London. Agreement thresholds were used to identify 47 final consensus statements.
paper.findings: The panel supported platelet-rich plasma for selected conditions such as patellar tendinopathy and symptomatic early osteoarthritis. It also highlighted inconsistent biologic preparation and reporting and cautioned that uncharacterized cell-based products are commonly promoted beyond the supporting evidence.
paper.limitations: Delphi agreement is expert opinion rather than a treatment trial, and participant selection can introduce bias. The recommendations reflect NFL physician experience and may not generalize to college athletes, other sports, different products, or different regulatory environments.
paper.practicalImplications: Require a condition-specific medical rationale, transparent product characterization, informed consent, and realistic discussion of uncertainty before using a biologic. Avoid broad claims that a product regenerates tissue or accelerates recovery when comparative evidence is absent.
paper.athleteDev: Biologics should not replace progressive loading, rehabilitation, sleep, nutrition, or workload management. When considered, integrate the intervention into a coordinated medical and performance plan with explicit outcome measures.
paper.rtp: A biologic injection is not a clearance criterion or a fixed recovery shortcut. Return-to-sport progression should remain based on tissue status, symptoms, function, sport demands, and response to graded loading.

records.sourceFile: What Performance Analysts Need to Know About Research Trends in Association Football (2012–2016)- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Sarmento H, Clemente FM, Araújo D, et al. What performance analysts need to know about research trends in association football (2012–2016): A systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(4):799-836.
paper.abstract: This systematic review mapped performance-analysis research on adult male association football published from 2012 through 2016, organizing 77 studies by tactical, technical, physical, contextual, and methodological themes.
paper.tldr: The literature concentrated on set pieces, collective behavior, match statistics and outcomes, activity profiles, fatigue and substitutions, plus environmental and situational constraints. The review helps analysts locate relevant evidence but does not validate a universal metric, model, or workflow.
paper.methods: Following PRISMA procedures, the authors screened 483 records and included 77 studies of adult male football match performance. Studies were categorized by research focus and their methods and findings were synthesized narratively.
paper.findings: Recurring themes included set-piece effectiveness, collective tactical behavior, associations between match statistics and outcomes, physical activity profiles, fatigue and substitution patterns, and effects of score line, venue, opposition, and environmental context.
paper.limitations: The search was limited to Web of Science and a five-year publication window. Included studies were heterogeneous, predominantly observational, and restricted to adult male football; mapping research activity is not the same as validating practical decision tools.
paper.practicalImplications: Frame match analysis around a specific decision and account for opponent, match state, venue, competition, and role. Combine tactical, technical, and physical information instead of treating a context-free count as a performance explanation.
paper.athleteDev: Use longitudinal, role-specific analysis to connect player behavior with team principles and development goals. A metric is most useful when its definition, context, and coaching response are consistent.
paper.rtp: The review does not validate return-to-sport thresholds. Match-analysis variables can help describe reintegration demands, but medical and functional readiness require separate evidence and individualized progression.

records.sourceFile: Acute First-Time Hamstring Strains During High-Speed Running A Longitudinal Study Including Clinical and Magnetic Resonance Imaging Findings.pdf

paper.citation: Askling CM, Tengvar M, Saartok T, Thorstensson A. Acute first-time hamstring strains during high-speed running. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(2):197-206.
paper.abstract: This longitudinal case series followed 18 elite sprinters after acute first-time hamstring strains sustained during high-speed running, combining serial clinical examination, magnetic resonance imaging, time to return, and two-year follow-up.
paper.tldr: All injuries involved the biceps femoris long head, and return to preinjury training ranged widely from 6 to 50 weeks, with a median of 16 weeks. Greater injury extent and involvement near the proximal free tendon were associated with longer recovery, but the small case series cannot supply a universal MRI-based timeline.
paper.methods: Athletes were assessed clinically and with magnetic resonance imaging approximately 2–4 days after injury and again around days 10, 21, and 42. Injury location and extent were compared with time to resume preinjury training, and athletes were followed for two years.
paper.findings: Every injury involved the long head of biceps femoris. Median time to return to preinjury training was 16 weeks, with a 6–50-week range. More extensive injury and proximity to or involvement of the proximal free tendon were associated with longer recovery.
paper.limitations: The study included only 18 elite sprinters, had no comparison group, and allowed rehabilitation to vary after the initial six weeks. Associations between MRI features and recovery do not create deterministic individual timelines or directly generalize to field-sport athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Expect substantial variation after high-speed-running hamstring injury and integrate mechanism, clinical function, loading response, and imaging when available. Communicate a range and update the forecast as running exposure progresses.
paper.athleteDev: Prepare athletes for progressive exposure to high-speed running and the specific force demands that precede sprinting. Prioritize capacity and graded exposure rather than assuming symptom resolution alone restores readiness.
paper.rtp: Proximal free-tendon involvement and greater injury extent may justify a more conservative forecast, but MRI should not determine clearance by itself. Progress running speed, volume, sprint mechanics, strength, symptoms, and sport-specific demands before unrestricted return.

records.sourceFile: The association between hip-groin pain and hip strength in football players - An exploratory analysis of the FORCe cohort.pdf

paper.citation: Bonello C, King MG, Crossley KM, et al. The association between hip/groin pain and hip strength in football players: An exploratory analysis of the FORCe cohort. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2023;26(9):471-475.
paper.abstract: This exploratory cross-sectional analysis compared hip-strength measures in football players with and without hip or groin pain and examined whether associations differed between soccer and Australian football participants.
paper.tldr: Symptomatic football players showed lower hip adduction, internal-rotation, and external-rotation strength than pain-free controls. Hip-abduction findings differed by sport, reinforcing that cross-sectional group differences are context dependent and cannot serve as causal, diagnostic, or prospective injury thresholds.
paper.methods: The analysis included 190 symptomatic players and 64 controls, representing 291 symptomatic limbs and 128 control limbs. Standardized hip-strength tests were compared by pain status, with exploratory evaluation of soccer and Australian-football subgroups.
paper.findings: Hip adduction, internal-rotation, and external-rotation strength were lower in limbs from players with hip or groin pain. Lower abduction strength was evident in Australian-football participants but not in soccer participants, suggesting a sport-specific association.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot determine whether weakness preceded or resulted from pain. Participants were subelite, pain presentations were mixed, limbs were analyzed within players, and observed group differences do not establish a diagnostic cutoff or future-injury prediction rule.
paper.practicalImplications: Assess hip strength as one part of a broader pain evaluation and compare athletes with their own repeated results and sport demands. A low value may identify a rehabilitation target, but it should not be interpreted as the cause of symptoms in isolation.
paper.athleteDev: Develop multi-planar hip capacity appropriate to the athlete's sport and position, while monitoring symptoms and movement tolerance. Avoid applying one sport's group reference or one isolated strength ratio to every football code.
paper.rtp: Track adduction and rotational strength alongside pain, function, running, cutting, kicking, and training tolerance. Clearance should reflect restored sport capacity rather than crossing an unvalidated single-test threshold.

records.sourceFile: The influence of sleep and training load on illness in nationally competitive male Australian Football athletes- a cohort study over one season.pdf

paper.citation: Fitzgerald D, Beckmans C, Joyce D, Mills K. The influence of sleep and training load on illness in nationally competitive male Australian Football athletes: A cohort study over one season. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019;22(2):130-134.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study followed 44 nationally competitive male Australian-football athletes across a 46-week season to examine associations among self-reported sleep, external training load, and subsequent illness.
paper.tldr: Across 67 recorded illnesses, shorter acute sleep quantity was the only independent factor associated with illness after the multivariable analysis; higher sleep was associated with lower odds. The finding supports routine sleep monitoring but does not prove that a sleep prescription will prevent illness.
paper.methods: Athletes reported sleep while external training load was monitored across 46 weeks. Acute and longer-window sleep and load variables were related to illness occurrence using multivariable statistical models.
paper.findings: The cohort recorded 67 illnesses. Acute sleep quantity remained independently associated with illness after adjustment, with an odds ratio of 0.49 (95% confidence interval 0.25–0.94); external-load measures were not independently associated when sleep was included.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, male, and limited to one sport and competitive level. Sleep was self-reported, illness and exposure relationships were observational, and residual confounding or reverse effects are possible. The odds ratio does not define an individual sleep cutoff.
paper.practicalImplications: Monitor recent sleep alongside load, symptoms, travel, and schedule pressure. When sleep falls below an athlete's normal pattern, investigate modifiable causes and coordinate recovery support rather than automatically reducing training from one value.
paper.athleteDev: Build consistent sleep routines and the skills to manage travel, late competition, academics, and stress. Use trends and athlete conversation to guide support instead of enforcing a universal number without context.
paper.rtp: During illness or injury, recent sleep can inform recovery planning but is not a clearance measure. Combine it with symptoms, medical status, functional progression, and tolerance of training exposure.

records.sourceFile: Between-Session Reliability of Field-Based Assessments of Isometric Neck Strength.pdf

paper.citation: Oxford SW, Clarke ND, Tallis J. Between-session reliability of field-based assessments of isometric neck strength. Sensors. 2024;24(15):5015.
paper.abstract: This methodological study evaluated between-session reliability of quadruped isometric neck-strength testing with VALD ForceFrame and DynaMo devices in 27 recreationally active men, including peak force and early force-development measures.
paper.tldr: Field-based quadruped neck-strength measures showed generally good between-session reliability, particularly for peak force, but early force-development metrics were more variable and the two devices should not be treated as interchangeable. Reliability supports repeat measurement; it does not establish injury prediction or a clearance threshold.
paper.methods: Twenty-seven recreationally active men completed repeated isometric neck-strength sessions using ForceFrame and DynaMo systems. Intraclass correlation coefficients, coefficients of variation, and agreement statistics quantified reliability across directions and force-time variables.
paper.findings: ForceFrame intraclass correlations exceeded 0.80 and DynaMo values exceeded 0.76, while coefficients of variation were below 13.8%. Peak-force measures were more stable than early force-development measures, and agreement did not support interchanging devices.
paper.limitations: Participants were healthy recreationally active men rather than contact-sport athletes or patients. The study evaluated reliability, not diagnostic validity, responsiveness, concussion risk, injury prevention, or return-to-play criteria; device-specific error must be respected.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the same device, setup, direction, instructions, and warm-up across sessions. Interpret changes against the measure's typical error and be more cautious with early force-development metrics than with peak force.
paper.athleteDev: If neck strength is monitored, establish an individual baseline and prioritize technically consistent, progressive training. Do not convert a reliable field test into an unsupported universal target or injury-risk label.
paper.rtp: Repeatable neck-strength testing may contribute to a broader cervical or contact-readiness assessment, but this study supplies no clearance cutoff. Use device-consistent trends with symptoms, examination, function, and graded contact exposure.

records.sourceFile: High‑Intensity Acceleration and Deceleration Demands in Elite Team Sports Competitive Match Play- A Systematic Review and Meta‑Analysis of Observational Studies.pdf

paper.citation: Harper DJ, Carling C, Kiely J. High-intensity acceleration and deceleration demands in elite team sports competitive match play: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. Sports Medicine. 2019;49(12):1923-1947.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 19 observational studies involving 469 elite male athletes across seven team sports to characterize high-intensity acceleration and deceleration demands during competition.
paper.tldr: High-intensity decelerations were generally more frequent than accelerations, except in American football, and soccer showed the largest imbalance. Large differences in thresholds, tracking systems, roles, and exposure definitions prevent a universal acceleration or deceleration dose from being transferred across sports or teams.
paper.methods: The authors pooled match-play observations from 19 studies across seven elite team sports. They compared frequencies and temporal patterns of high-intensity acceleration and deceleration while evaluating methodological differences among global-positioning and tracking approaches.
paper.findings: Decelerations occurred more often than accelerations in most included sports, with American football as an exception and soccer showing the largest acceleration-deceleration imbalance. Pooled data also suggested small declines in high-intensity actions during the second half.
paper.limitations: Definitions, thresholds, sampling and processing methods, exposure units, playing positions, and sport demands varied substantially. Evidence was limited to elite adult men and observational match data, so pooled values do not prescribe an optimal training dose or individual readiness target.
paper.practicalImplications: Create sport-, position-, and system-specific reference distributions with stable processing rules. Prepare athletes for both propulsive and braking demands and track how exposure is accumulated, not merely the total number of events.
paper.athleteDev: Progress acceleration and deceleration exposure through technique, strength, tissue capacity, and representative movement tasks. Use match demands to frame preparation while individualizing for role, training age, and current tolerance.
paper.rtp: Reintroduce acceleration and especially deceleration demands progressively, using the athlete's sport and position as context. Avoid declaring readiness from a generic event count or threshold derived from another tracking system.

records.sourceFile: Mediterranean Diet and athletic performance in elite and competitive athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Fiorini S, Guglielmetti M, Neri LCL, et al. Mediterranean diet and athletic performance in elite and competitive athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutrition, Metabolism and Cardiovascular Diseases. 2025;35(11):104165.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated Mediterranean-diet adherence and performance in elite and competitive athletes. Nine small, predominantly male studies were included, with five cross-sectional studies examining diet-performance relationships.
paper.tldr: Most individual relationship studies favored higher Mediterranean-diet adherence, but the pooled performance effect was null: standardized mean difference 0.00 (95% confidence interval -0.26 to 0.25). The evidence supports a healthful food pattern more strongly than a guaranteed direct performance gain.
paper.methods: Nine studies involving 192 athletes were reviewed, and eligible performance outcomes were pooled. Study designs, adherence measures, sports, and performance tests varied, with five studies using cross-sectional association designs.
paper.findings: Four of five studies examining relationships reported favorable associations between Mediterranean-diet adherence and some performance outcomes. However, the meta-analysis found no pooled performance difference, with a standardized mean difference of 0.00 and a 95% confidence interval from -0.26 to 0.25.
paper.limitations: The evidence base was small, mostly male, heterogeneous, and low to moderate in quality; many studies were cross-sectional. Dietary assessment and performance outcomes differed, and supplement use was often not adequately measured. Causality and sport-specific effects remain uncertain.
paper.practicalImplications: A Mediterranean-style pattern can guide food quality and variety, but performance nutrition still requires adequate total energy, carbohydrate availability, protein distribution, hydration, and sport-specific timing. Do not promise a direct performance boost from adherence alone.
paper.athleteDev: Use the pattern as a flexible foundation built around vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, olive oil, fish, and minimally processed foods, then individualize portions and timing to training demands, preferences, access, and tolerance.
paper.rtp: During rehabilitation, the dietary pattern may support general health, but it is not a treatment or clearance tool. Ensure adequate energy and protein for healing and coordinate individualized needs with qualified sports-nutrition and medical staff.

records.sourceFile: Adherence to Strength Training and Lower Rates of Sports Injury in Contact Sports - A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Chen Z, Wang J, Zhao K, He G. Adherence to strength training and lower rates of sports injury in contact sports: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(5):23259671251331134.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 16 randomized controlled trials of strength-training interventions intended to reduce injuries in contact-sport participants, including single-component and multicomponent programs.
paper.tldr: Strength-training interventions were associated with a 30% lower pooled injury rate, but programs, sports, adherence, and outcome definitions varied. The result supports consistently delivered strength exposure as part of prevention; it does not identify one universally superior exercise, dose, or program.
paper.methods: Sixteen randomized controlled trials were included and injury risk ratios were pooled. Analyses examined overall effects and subgroups based on single-component or multicomponent programs and injury location.
paper.findings: The pooled injury risk ratio was 0.70 (95% confidence interval 0.60–0.82). Single-component analyses reported lower groin-injury risk (0.69) and hamstring-injury risk (0.37), while multicomponent analyses reported lower knee-injury risk (0.71) and ankle-injury risk (0.68).
paper.limitations: Sports, participant characteristics, program content, dose, adherence, exposure, and injury definitions varied. Subgroup findings do not directly compare components or prove superiority, and the review provides insufficient detail for one universal prescription.
paper.practicalImplications: Protect regular, progressive strength-training exposure and track completion, quality, and tolerance. Select exercises and doses for the sport's injury patterns and the athlete's needs, then adapt without losing the program's essential loading stimulus.
paper.athleteDev: Embed strength development across the year instead of relying on short prevention blocks. Sustainable adherence, progressive overload, and technically sound execution are more defensible targets than copying a single pooled protocol.
paper.rtp: Rebuild relevant strength capacity progressively and transition from rehabilitation exercises to representative contact-sport loading. The pooled prevention effect does not define a clearance threshold or replace functional and sport-specific testing.
